where: Section 3 (why the CE stage is slow)
problem: The arithmetic does not support the stated result. "Hundreds of pF times a few kΩ" gives about 1–2 μs, so 1/(2πτ) is roughly 100–160 kHz, which is in the hundreds of kHz, not "tens of kHz". A student who checks the numbers will think the estimate is wrong.
fix: Write: hundreds of pF times a few kΩ gives a time constant around a microsecond, so fH falls to a few hundred kHz, and with a high-resistance source it can drop to tens of kHz.

problem: "Only a few pF load the input" understates the CB input. In CB the input is the emitter and Cπ (10–200 pF by this chapter's own numbers) sits from emitter to ground, so it does load the input. What CB avoids is the Miller multiplication of Cμ, not capacitive loading altogether.
fix: Write: the input is loaded by Cπ alone (10–200 pF, no multiplication); Cμ runs from collector to ground and is not multiplied, so the input pole sits far higher than in CE.

problem: The edge from C_M to the gain stage labelled "drives" makes C_M look like a series element carrying the signal into the amplifier. C_M is a shunt capacitance at the input node; the amplifier input is that same node. A student can misread the block diagram.
fix: Feed the gain stage directly from the input node, and draw C_M as a shunt branch from the input node to ground, with the dashed feedback edge from the output back to that node.
